Prealgebra · Lesson 10.3

Casework

Solve this lesson →All lessons

One multiply only works when the choices stay the same all the way across. When they change partway through, split what you are counting into separate cases, count each case on its own, and add the counts.

Problem
A food truck sells tacos (with 11 of 55 fillings) and burritos (with 11 of 44 fillings and 11 of 22 salsas). How many different single items can you order?
Show a hint
  • You cannot count this with one clean multiply, because a taco has just one choice to make and a burrito has two. So split it. What are the two separate piles of items you are choosing from?
  • Make two cases, one for tacos and one for burritos. A taco is fully decided by its single filling. A burrito is decided by its filling and its salsa together. Count each case on its own.
  • Tacos give you 55 ways. For burritos you pick one of 44 fillings and one of 22 salsas, which is 4×2=84×2=8 ways. Now you just have the two pile counts 55 and 88 sitting in front of you.
Show the full solution
There are 55 tacos, one for each filling. A burrito needs a filling and a salsa, so there are 4×2=84×2=8 burritos. Nothing is both, so add the two piles, 5+8=13.5+8=13. You can order 1313​ different items. One multiply cannot handle this in one shot, since a taco makes one choice and a burrito makes two. Multiply inside a case, add across cases.
Problem
Zedland has a 6-letter alphabet. Words can be 1, 2, or 3 letters long, with repeats allowed. How many possible words are there?
Show a hint
  • The words come in different lengths, and a one-letter word and a three-letter word are built in very different ways. Try splitting the count by how long the word is, so you handle each length on its own.
  • Set up three piles. Count the one-letter words, then the two-letter words, then the three-letter words. Inside each pile every slot has 66 choices, so a one-letter word has 66 options, a two-letter word has 6×66×6, and a three-letter word has 6×6×66×6×6.
  • Work out each pile and you get 66 one-letter words, 62=3662=36 two-letter words, and 63=21663=216 three-letter words. All that is left is to add the three pile counts together.
Show the full solution
Count by length. One-letter words give 66, two-letter words give 62=3662=36, and three-letter words give 63=21663=216. A word has exactly one length, so the piles do not overlap and you add, 6+36+216=258.6+36+216=258. There are 258258​ possible words. Inside a case every slot has 66 choices, so you multiply. Across the cases you add.
Problem
Using the map above, there are 44 routes from A to D, and from D to H there are 33 routes (via E, via F, or direct). How many routes go all the way from A to H?
Show a hint
  • The whole trip squeezes through one town. Every route from AA to HH has to pass through DD, so split the route at DD into the first stretch AA to DD and the second stretch DD to HH, and handle each pile on its own.
  • You are told the first stretch AA to DD has 44 routes. Now count the second stretch DD to HH by listing its cases. There is DD to EE to HH, there is DD to FF to HH, and there is the direct road DD to HH.
  • So the second stretch has 33 routes. Picking a way from AA to DD and then a way from DD to HH are two independent choices, so this is a multiply, not an add. You just need 4×34×3.
Show the full solution
From DD to HH there are 33 routes, one through EE, one through FF, and the direct road. Each of the 44 routes from AA to DD can be followed by any of those, so 4×3=12.4×3=12. There are 1212​ routes from AA to HH. Every route passes through DD, which is why the trip splits there. The two halves are independent, so this step is a multiply, not an add.
Key idea
Casework. When a single multiplication will not work because the choices change partway through, split what you are counting into a few cases, count each case separately, then add the case counts. Inside one case the choices are fixed, so you multiply straight across as in 10.2. Across the cases you add, as in 10.1. Two conditions must hold. The cases must not overlap, or something is counted twice. Together they must cover every outcome, or something is left out.
Problem
Every whole number from 11 to 150150 is written out. How many digits are written in total?
Show a hint
  • One clean multiply will not work here, because the numbers are not all the same length. The number 77 uses one digit, 4343 uses two, and 128128 uses three. So split your count into piles by how many digits each number has.
  • Make three piles. The one-digit numbers run from 11 to 99, the two-digit numbers run from 1010 to 9999, and the three-digit numbers run from 100100 to 150150. Inside each pile, count how many numbers there are and multiply by the digits each one uses.
  • Pile one gives 9×1=99×1=9 digits, pile two gives 90×2=18090×2=180 digits, and pile three gives 51×3=15351×3=153 digits. Now you just need to bring the three pile counts together.
Show the full solution
Split by how many digits a number has. The numbers 11 to 99 are 99 numbers with 11 digit each, so 9×1=99×1=9. The numbers 1010 to 9999 are 9090 numbers with 22 digits each, so 90×2=18090×2=180. The numbers 100100 to 150150 are 5151 numbers with 33 digits each, so 51×3=15351×3=153. Adding the piles, 9+180+153=342,9+180+153=342, so you write 342342​ digits. The piles never overlap and together cover every number, so nothing is counted twice and nothing slips through.
Problem
How many two-digit numbers have a tens digit greater than the units digit?
Show a hint
  • You cannot just multiply choices for the two digits, because once you pick the tens digit, the number of allowed units digits depends on what you picked. Try splitting the count by the tens digit, and handle each tens digit as its own pile.
  • Pick a tens digit and call it tt. It can be anything from 11 to 99. For that fixed tt, the units digit just has to be smaller, so it can be 0,1,…,t−10,1,…,t−1, which is tt choices.
  • So the tens digit t=1t=1 gives 11 number, t=2t=2 gives 22 numbers, on up to t=9t=9 giving 99 numbers. Now you just need the total of 1+2+⋯+91+2+⋯+9.
Show the full solution
Case on the tens digit tt. The units digit only has to be smaller, so it can be 0,1,…,t−10,1,…,t−1, which is tt choices. Running tt from 11 to 99 and adding gives 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8+9=45,1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8+9=45, so there are 4545​ such numbers. You cannot just multiply 9×109×10 here, because how many units digits are allowed depends on which tens digit you picked.
Problem
Hat 1 holds balls numbered 11 to 1515 and Hat 2 holds balls 1616 to 2525. You pick one hat, then draw 22 balls from it one after another without replacement, where order matters. How many different ordered draws are possible?
Show a hint
  • The two hats hold different amounts of balls, so one clean multiply will not work for the whole thing at once. Try splitting the count by which hat you reached into.
  • Set up two piles. In the hat one pile you draw from 1515 balls, and in the hat two pile you draw from 1010 balls. Count the ordered draws in each pile on its own.
  • Hat one gives 15×14=21015×14=210 ordered draws and hat two gives 10×9=9010×9=90 ordered draws. Now you just need to put the two pile counts together.
Show the full solution
Split by hat. Hat 1 holds 1515 balls, so the two draws give 15×14=21015×14=210. Hat 2 holds 1010 balls, so 10×9=9010×9=90. A draw comes from exactly one hat, so add, 210+90=300.210+90=300. That is 300300​ ordered draws. The second factor drops by one because the first ball stays out. The hats hold different amounts, which is why one multiply cannot cover both at once.
Problem
Using pennies, nickels, and dimes (any amounts, including zero), how many ways can you make 2020 cents?
Show a hint
  • One clean multiply will not work here, because the coins are not interchangeable. Try splitting the problem into piles based on the coin that limits you the most. Since dimes are the biggest, ask how many dimes you use and make a separate case for each choice.
  • Figure out which numbers of dimes are even possible. You can use 00 dimes, 11 dime, or 22 dimes, since 33 dimes would already be 3030 cents, which is too much. So you have exactly three cases to count, one for each of those dime counts.
  • In each case, count how many nickels can fit in the leftover amount, and let pennies quietly fill whatever is still missing. With 00 dimes you have 2020 cents to fill, so nickels can be 0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3, or 44. With 11 dime you have 1010 cents left, so nickels can be 0,1,0,1, or 22. With 22 dimes you have 00 cents left, so nickels must be 00. Now you just need to add the three pile counts together.
Show the full solution
Case on the number of dimes. With 00 dimes there is 2020 cents to fill, so the nickels can be 0,1,2,3,0,1,2,3, or 44 and pennies fill the rest, which is 55 ways. With 11 dime there is 1010 cents left, so nickels can be 0,1,0,1, or 22, which is 33 ways. With 22 dimes nothing is left, which is 11 way. Three dimes is already 3030 cents, too much. Adding, 5+3+1=9,5+3+1=9, so there are 99​ ways. Split on the coin that boxes you in the most, here the dime. Once the dimes and nickels are set, the pennies are forced, so there is nothing left to choose.
Key idea
Choosing what to split on. You pick the cases yourself, and a good choice gives the fewest and cleanest cases. Split on the most constrained part of the problem, like the largest coin you can spend or a digit that a rule fixes. If one choice changes how many ways the rest can go, split on that choice first. Then lay the cases out in a table or list and add straight down the column, so no case is skipped and none is counted twice.
Problem
How many ordered pairs of positive integers (a,b)(a,b) satisfy a2+b<24a2+b<24?
Show a hint
  • Try the slot method and you will notice the choices for bb shrink as aa grows, so one clean multiply will not work. Split into cases by the value of aa instead, and count each value on its own.
  • Pin down aa first. If a=1a=1 then you need 1+b<241+b<24, so b<23b<23. If a=2a=2 then 4+b<244+b<24, so b<20b<20. Keep going for a=3a=3 and a=4a=4, and check where a2a2 alone already pushes past 2424.
  • Count the allowed bb values in each case, remembering bb starts at 11. You should get 2222 for a=1a=1, then 1919, then 1414, then 77, and nothing for a=5a=5. Now add those pile counts.
Show the full solution
Case on aa. With a=1a=1 we need 1+b<241+b<24, so b<23b<23 and bb runs 11 to 2222, which is 2222 pairs. With a=2a=2, b<20b<20 gives 1919 pairs. With a=3a=3, b<15b<15 gives 1414. With a=4a=4, b<8b<8 gives 77. At a=5a=5 we already have a2=25a2=25, too big on its own, so we stop. Adding, 22+19+14+7=62,22+19+14+7=62, so there are 6262​ pairs. The room left for bb shrinks as aa grows, so no single multiply works. Watch the endpoint too, since b<23b<23 means 2222 values, not 2323.
Problem
How many two-digit numbers have digits that add up to a perfect square?
Show a hint
  • The slot method from 10.2 will not work here in one clean multiply, because the digit sum can land on a few different perfect squares and each one behaves differently. So split into cases by the digit sum. First figure out which perfect squares a digit sum can even reach.
  • The two digits of a two-digit number add up to somewhere between 11 and 1818. The perfect squares living in that range are 11, 44, 99, and 1616. Make one case for each of those four sums, then count the two-digit numbers in each case on its own.
  • Sum =1=1 gives just 1010, so 11 number. Sum =4=4 gives 44 numbers, and sum =9=9 gives 99 numbers. Sum =16=16 gives 33 numbers. Now add the four pile counts the way you added in 10.1.
Show the full solution
Two digits add to somewhere between 11 and 1818, so the perfect squares in reach are 11, 44, 99, and 1616. Sum 11 gives only 1010, so 11 number. Sum 44 gives 1313, 2222, 3131, 4040, so 44. Sum 99 gives 1818, 2727, 3636, 4545, 5454, 6363, 7272, 8181, 9090, so 99. Sum 1616 gives 7979, 8888, 9797, so 33. Adding, 1+4+9+3=17,1+4+9+3=17, so there are 1717​ numbers. Pinning down which sums are even reachable is most of the work. Miss one square and the count comes up short.
Problem
How many three-digit numbers have exactly one digit equal to 00?
Show a hint
  • The leading digit of a three-digit number can never be 00, since a number like 047047 is really just 4747. So the lone 00 has nowhere to hide in the hundreds spot. That tells you the two places where the single 00 could actually sit, and those two spots are a perfect thing to split into cases on.
  • Make two cases. In the first case the 00 sits in the tens place and the units digit is not 00. In the second case the 00 sits in the units place and the tens digit is not 00. Inside each case, figure out how many choices the hundreds digit has and how many choices the remaining free digit has, then multiply those two counts.
  • Case one gives 9×9=819×9=81, and case two gives 9×9=819×9=81. The two cases never overlap and together they cover every way to have exactly one 00. All that is left is to combine the two pile counts.
Show the full solution
The hundreds digit is never 00, since 061061 is really just 6161. So the lone 00 sits in the tens place or the units place. With the 00 in the tens place, the hundreds digit has 99 choices and the units digit has 99, giving 9×9=819×9=81. The 00 in the units place works the same way, another 8181. Adding, 81+81=162,81+81=162, so there are 162162​ numbers. The other free digit has to be nonzero, or you would have two zeros instead of exactly one.
Problem
How many three-digit numbers have a hundreds digit that is at least 33 times the tens digit?
Show a hint
  • The rule only ties together the hundreds digit and the tens digit, and the units digit is free with all 1010 choices no matter what. So the tidiest thing to split on is the tens digit tt, because once you fix tt the demand "hundreds is at least 3t3t" becomes one simple count.
  • Walk the tens digit through its values and ask how many hundreds digits from 11 to 99 clear the bar 3t3t. When t=0t=0 you need hundreds at least 00, so all of 11 to 99 work. When t=1t=1 you need hundreds at least 33. When t=2t=2 you need at least 66. When t=3t=3 you need at least 99. When tt is 44 or more, even 99 is too small, so those cases give nothing.
  • Count the hundreds choices in each living case, then remember every one of those still gets 1010 free units digits. You should have hundreds counts of 99, 77, 44, and 11 for t=0,1,2,3t=0,1,2,3. Add those, then multiply by 1010.
Show the full solution
Case on the tens digit tt. The units digit never appears in the rule, so it always brings 1010 choices. For t=0t=0 the hundreds digit needs to be at least 00, so all 99 work. For t=1t=1 it must be at least 33, so 77 work. For t=2t=2, at least 66, so 44. For t=3t=3, at least 99, so 11. For t=4t=4 or more you would need a digit of 1212 or bigger, so those piles are empty. That gives 9+7+4+1=219+7+4+1=21 hundreds-tens pairs, each carrying 1010 units digits, so 21×10=210.21×10=210. The count is 210210​. A digit no rule touches just multiplies in at the end. Pull it out early and the casework gets much shorter.
Key idea
Counting by complement. Sometimes the two cases are the outcomes that have the property and the outcomes that do not. The second group is the complement of the first. When the complement is easier to count, count it and subtract from the total. That is the same total minus the rest move from 10.1, and it handles at least one questions.
Problem
How many whole numbers from 11 to 999999 have at least one digit equal to 22?
Show a hint
  • Counting the numbers that DO have a 22 splits into messy overlapping cases, the 22 could be in the ones, the tens, or the hundreds place, and some numbers have it in more than one spot. The slick split is just has a 22 versus does not have a 22. Count the friendlier side, the ones with no 22 at all, and subtract from the total.
  • Picture every number from 11 to 999999 as three digit slots, like 007007 for 77 or 052052 for 5252. For a slot to avoid the digit 22, it can be any of {0,1,3,4,5,6,7,8,9}{0,1,3,4,5,6,7,8,9}, which is 99 choices. Multiply the slots the 10.2 way to count all three-slot strings with no 22.
  • Three slots with 99 choices each gives 9×9×9=7299×9×9=729 strings from 000000 to 999999 that avoid the digit 22. But 000000 is really 00, which is not in 11 to 999999, so toss it and you have 728728 numbers with no 22. The total count of numbers is 999999. Now you only need one subtraction.
Show the full solution
Count the numbers with no 22 instead. Write every number as three slots, so 77 is 007007 and 5252 is 052052. A slot dodging the 22 has 99 choices, giving 9×9×9=7299×9×9=729 strings from 000000 to 999999. Drop 000000, which stands for 00 and is not in the range, leaving 728728. There are 999999 numbers in all, so 999−728=271,999−728=271, and 271271​ of them have at least one 22. Counting the 22s head on means overlapping cases, since a number can carry two or three of them. Counting the other side avoids all of that.
Fun fact
In 1976 two mathematicians settled the Four Color Map Theorem using pure casework, they reduced every possible map to one of about 1,976 basic shapes and had a computer check each one.
Key idea
How to do casework. When a single multiplication will not count everything, choose what to split on, usually the most restricted part of the problem. Your cases must not overlap and must cover every possibility, so nothing is counted twice and nothing is missed. Count each case on its own, multiplying inside a case as in 10.2, then add the case counts as in 10.1. In 10.4 Counting Pairs we count how many ways to choose a pair or group when order does not matter, so picking Sam then Maya is the same choice as Maya then Sam.

Practice these ideas

Practice
A small sundae has 55 flavor choices. A large has 55 flavors and 22 sauces. How many different sundaes can you order?
Show the solution
A small sundae is just a flavor, so there are 55 of them. A large is a flavor and a sauce, so 5×2=105×2=10. No sundae is both sizes, so add, 5+10=15.5+10=15. There are 1515​ different sundaes. Multiply inside a case, add across the cases.
Practice
A code is 11 or 22 symbols long, each from 55 shapes, with repeats allowed. How many possible codes are there?
Show the solution
Split by length. A 11-symbol code has one slot with 55 shapes, so 55 codes. A 22-symbol code has two slots with 55 shapes each, so 52=2552=25 codes. A code has exactly one length, so add, 5+25=30.5+25=30. There are 3030​ possible codes. When the things you are counting come in different lengths, one multiply cannot reach them all. Split by length first.
Practice
Every whole number from 11 to 9999 is written out. How many digits are written in total?
Show the solution
Split by how many digits a number has. The numbers 11 to 99 are 99 numbers with one digit each, so 99 digits. The numbers 1010 to 9999 are 9090 numbers with two digits each, so 90×2=18090×2=180 digits. Adding, 9+180=189,9+180=189, so 189189​ digits are written. A 77 costs one digit and a 5353 costs two, so there is no single length to multiply by.
Practice
Using pennies, nickels, and dimes (any amounts, including zero), how many ways can you make 3030 cents?
Show the solution
Case on the number of dimes, which can be 00, 11, 22, or 33. Once the dimes and nickels are chosen the pennies are forced, so only the nickels need counting. With 3030 cents left you can use 00 up to 66 nickels, which is 77 ways. With 2020 cents left, 00 up to 44 nickels, which is 55 ways. With 1010 cents left, 33 ways. With 00 cents left, 11 way. Adding, 7+5+3+1=16,7+5+3+1=16, so there are 1616​ ways. Split on the biggest coin. It has the fewest possible values, so it pins the rest down fastest.
Practice
How many ordered pairs of positive integers (a,b)(a,b) satisfy a2+b<15a2+b<15?
Show the solution
Case on aa. Since bb is at least 11, we need a2<14a2<14, so aa can only be 11, 22, or 33. With a=1a=1 we need b<14b<14, so bb runs 11 to 1313, which is 1313 pairs. With a=2a=2, b<11b<11 gives 1010 pairs. With a=3a=3, b<6b<6 gives 55 pairs. Adding, 13+10+5=28,13+10+5=28, so there are 2828​ pairs. Checking which aa are even possible first keeps the case list short and stops you from hunting past a=3a=3.
Practice
How many two-digit numbers have a units digit strictly greater than the tens digit?
Show the solution
Case on the tens digit tt. The units digit must be bigger, so it runs from t+1t+1 up to 99, which is 9−t9−t choices. That gives 88 when t=1t=1, 77 when t=2t=2, and so on down to 11 when t=8t=8, with nothing left at t=9t=9. Adding, 8+7+6+5+4+3+2+1=36,8+7+6+5+4+3+2+1=36, so there are 3636​ such numbers. Each case count shrinks by one, so the whole total is just 11 through 88 added up.
Practice
How many three-digit numbers have a hundreds digit that is at least 22 times the tens digit?
Show the solution
Case on the tens digit tt, with the units digit free at 1010 choices throughout. We need the hundreds digit hh from 11 to 99 with h≥2th≥2t. For t=0t=0 all 99 work. For t=1t=1 we need h≥2h≥2, so 88 work. For t=2t=2 we need h≥4h≥4, so 66. For t=3t=3 we need h≥6h≥6, so 44. For t=4t=4 we need h≥8h≥8, so 22. From t=5t=5 on you would need h≥10h≥10, which no digit reaches. So (9+8+6+4+2)×10=29×10=290,(9+8+6+4+2)×10=29×10=290, giving 290290​ numbers. The units digit never appears in the rule, so pull its 1010 choices out and multiply them in at the end.
Practice
How many three-digit numbers have a hundreds digit equal to the sum of the tens and units digits?
Show the solution
Case on the hundreds digit hh, which runs from 11 to 99. With hh fixed, the tens digit can be anything from 00 up to hh and the units digit is forced to be whatever is left, so that is h+1h+1 ways. Adding over h=1h=1 through h=9h=9, 2+3+4+⋯+10=54,2+3+4+⋯+10=54, so there are 5454​ numbers. Split on the digit the rule pins down. Here hh sets the target sum, and then one choice forces the other.
Practice
Box 1 has 88 cards, Box 2 has 66. Pick a box, then draw 22 cards in order without replacement. How many ordered draws are possible?
Show the solution
Split by box. Box 1 has 88 cards, so 8×7=568×7=56 ordered draws. Box 2 has 66 cards, so 6×5=306×5=30. A draw comes from one box only, so add, 56+30=86.56+30=86. There are 8686​ ordered draws. The second factor drops by one because the first card is not put back.
Practice
How many four-digit numbers have exactly one digit equal to 00?
Show the solution
The thousands digit is never 00, so the lone 00 sits in the hundreds, tens, or ones spot, which gives 33 cases. Take the 00 in the hundreds spot. The thousands digit has 99 choices, and the tens and ones must each be nonzero for 99 choices each, so that case is 9×9×9=7299×9×9=729. The other two cases work out the same, so 3×729=2187,3×729=2187, giving 21872187​ numbers. A number lands in one case only, decided by where its single 00 sits. When every case is the same size, adding them is just multiplying by the number of cases.
Practice
How many whole numbers from 11 to 500500 have at least one digit equal to 77?
Show the solution
Count the numbers with no 77 instead. Write each number from 00 to 499499 as three slots. The hundreds slot is 00 through 44 and none of those is a 77, so 55 choices, while the tens and ones slots each have 99 choices once 77 is banned. That is 5×9×9=4055×9×9=405 strings. One of them is 000000, which is outside our range, but 500500 has no 77 and belongs in the pile, so the two adjustments cancel and 405−1+1=405405−1+1=405 numbers from 11 to 500500 avoid the digit 77. Everything else has one, so 500−405=95,500−405=95, giving 9595​ numbers. Counting the 77s head on means overlapping cases, since 7777 would get caught twice. Counting the other side sidesteps that.
Practice
A 3-character code has exactly one digit (1010 choices) and two letters (2626 choices each). How many such codes are there?
Show the solution
Split on which spot holds the digit, which gives 33 cases. With the digit first, that spot has 1010 choices and the two letter spots have 2626 each, so 10×26×26=676010×26×26=6760 codes. The digit in the second or third spot gives 67606760 each as well, so 3×6760=20280,3×6760=20280, giving 2028020280​ codes. Every code has its digit in exactly one spot, so the three cases do not overlap and nothing is counted twice.
Practice
How many three-digit numbers have digits that add up to 44?
Show the solution
Case on the hundreds digit hh, which must be at least 11 and at most 44 or the sum overshoots. With hh fixed, the tens and units digits must add to 4−h4−h, and a target sum of ss allows s+1s+1 pairs, since the tens digit runs 00 up to ss and the units digit is forced. So h=1h=1 gives 44 ways, h=2h=2 gives 33, h=3h=3 gives 22, and h=4h=4 gives 11. Adding, 4+3+2+1=10,4+3+2+1=10, so there are 1010​ numbers. Split on the most cramped digit. The hundreds digit is squeezed from both sides here, which keeps the case list to four.
Practice
How many ordered pairs of positive integers (a,b)(a,b) satisfy a+b2<20a+b2<20?
Show the solution
Case on bb, since the rule rearranges to a<20−b2a<20−b2. With b=1b=1 we need a<19a<19, so 1818 values. With b=2b=2, a<16a<16 gives 1515. With b=3b=3, a<11a<11 gives 1010. With b=4b=4, a<4a<4 gives 33. At b=5b=5 we have b2=25b2=25, already too big on its own, so the cases stop. Adding, 18+15+10+3=46,18+15+10+3=46, so there are 4646​ pairs. Split on the squared variable, because it is the one that eats the room fastest and so gives the fewest cases.
